o: Each stock i costs present[i] and later sells for future[i], yielding profit future[i] − present[i] (possibly negative). With a budget, choose a subset maximizing total profit — a classic 0/1 knapsack where weight = price and value = profit. Example 1 picks stocks 0, 3, 4 costing exactly 10 for profit 6. Example 3 shows buying nothing (profit 0) can be optimal. Budget ≤ 1000 and prices ≤ 100 make tabulation cheap.
k: This is 0/1 knapsack: item weight = present[i], item value = future[i] − present[i].
Skip items with non-positive profit implicitly — the DP handles it since taking them never helps (or filter them first).
Iterate budgets downward for the 1D optimization so each stock is used at most once.

a.i: dp[b] = best profit using at most b money. For each stock, iterate b from budget down to price, setting dp[b] = max(dp[b], dp[b − price] + profit). The reverse iteration guarantees each stock is taken at most once.
s: For each stock with price p and profit g = future[i] − present[i]: for b from budget down to p, dp[b] = max(dp[b], dp[b−p] + g).
a.t: O(n · budget) ≈ 10^6 — each stock relaxes all feasible budgets.

a.i: The textbook formulation dp[i][b] = best profit using the first i stocks with budget b, with dp[i][b] = max(dp[i-1][b], dp[i-1][b-p]+g). Easier to explain and extend (e.g., reconstruction), at the cost of O(n · budget) memory.
s: For each stock i and budget b: carry dp[i-1][b]; if b ≥ p, also try dp[i-1][b-p] + g.
a.t: O(n · budget) — filling the full table.

w: Use the 1D version as your primary answer; mention 2D if asked to recover the chosen subset. Pitfalls: iterating the budget upward in the 1D version (allows re-buying the same stock — unbounded knapsack bug), and forgetting that profit can be negative so 'buy nothing' (0) must remain achievable. Follow-up: what if you could buy fractional shares? Then it becomes a greedy density problem.
